target: Je descendais les escaliers quatre à quatre.
english: I used to run down the stairs.
tip: 'Quatre à quatre' literally means 'four by four' – the image is taking the stairs four steps at a time, i.e. bounding down them fast.

target: Il pouvait courir très vite à cette époque.
english: He used to be able to run very fast at that time.
tip: 'Il pouvait courir' = he was able to, a standing ability. Switch to 'il a pu' and it means he managed to, that one time.

target: Je me lève à sept heures tous les matins.
english: I get up at seven o'clock every morning.
tip: Reflexive verbs use a pronoun: me, te, se, nous, vous, se. Je me lève = I get myself up.

target: Tu avais faim quand tu es rentré du travail ?
english: Were you hungry when you came home from work?
tip: Feelings live in the imparfait: 'avais faim' (were hungry) is the ongoing state, 'es rentré' (came home) the completed action framing it.

target: Tu avais dix ans quand tu as déménagé en France ?
english: Were you ten years old when you moved to France?
tip: Age in the past is always imparfait: 'tu avais dix ans' = you were ten. The move, 'as déménagé', is the one-off event.

target: Elle faisait la cuisine quand elle s'est coupé le doigt.
english: She was cooking when she cut her finger.
tip: No -e on 'coupé' here: in 'elle s'est coupé le doigt' the finger is the real object, so the participle doesn't agree with elle.

target: Tu t'es fait mal ?
english: Did you hurt yourself?
tip: Se faire mal literally means 'make yourself hurt' – French builds hurting from faire (to make), not from a verb 'to hurt'. Tu t'es fait mal? = did you make yourself hurt?

target: Je me suis trompé de route.
english: I took the wrong road.
tip: 'Se tromper de' + noun = to get the wrong one: 'je me suis trompé de route' = I took the wrong road.

target: Elle s'est excusée pour son retard.
english: She apologized for being late.
tip: To apologize is to excuse yourself in French: s'excuser. Elle s'est excusée = she excused herself. There's no separate verb for 'apologize'.

target: Tu te sens bien aujourd'hui ?
english: Do you feel well today?
tip: Feeling takes a reflexive here: se sentir. Tu te sens bien? adds a te ('yourself') that English drops – you don't just feel, you feel yourself.

target: Elles se telephonent tous les jours.
english: They call each other every day.
tip: This se means 'each other', not 'themselves': elles se téléphonent = they phone each other. The same little word covers reflexive and reciprocal – context decides which.

target: Il pleuvait quand nous sommes sortis.
english: It was raining when we went out.
tip: The imparfait is the backdrop, the passé composé the event: 'il pleuvait' (was raining) when 'nous sommes sortis' (we went out).

target: Elle s'est blessée en faisant du ski.
english: She hurt herself while skiing.
tip: En plus the -ant form means 'while doing': en faisant du ski = while skiing. It's French's compact way to pin one action to another going on at the same time.

target: Il s'est cassé le bras en tombant.
english: He broke his arm falling.
tip: French says the arm, not his arm, for body parts: il s'est cassé le bras. The reflexive se already tells you whose it is, so a possessive would be redundant.

target: Tu peux le faire pour demain ?
english: Can you do it by tomorrow?
tip: Pour here means 'by', a deadline, not 'for': pour demain = by tomorrow. French reuses the same pour for purpose and for due-dates.

target: Il est parti sans que je le sache.
english: He left without me knowing.
tip: Sans que ('without') forces the subjunctive: sans que je le sache, not sais. Some conjunctions flip the verb to subjunctive no matter how factual it feels.

target: Tu te souviens de notre première rencontre ?
english: Do you remember our first meeting?
tip: Remembering is reflexive in French and drags 'de' along: 'tu te souviens de...' = do you remember...? Literally 'you remind yourself of'.

target: Nous étions très fatigués mais nous avons continué à marcher.
english: We were very tired but we kept walking.
tip: Continuer needs à before the next verb: continuer à marcher = keep walking. Lots of French verbs pin a following infinitive with à or de, not directly.

target: Il faut que l'on prenne le train de six heures.
english: We need to take the six o'clock train.
tip: 'Il faut que' forces the subjunctive: it's 'prenne', not 'prend'. Necessity plus que changes the verb's form.

target: Ils jouaient dans le jardin quand il a commencé à pleuvoir.
english: They were playing in the garden when it started raining.
tip: 'Quand' or 'lorsque' + passé composé marks the interrupting event. The other action is imparfait.

target: Il s'intéressé à l'art contemporain.
english: He is interested in contemporary art.
tip: You're interested à something in French, not 'in' it: s'intéresser à. Il s'intéresse à l'art = interested in art. The verb picks à and the English 'in' vanishes.

target: Il se plaint toujours du temps.
english: He always complains about the weather.
tip: Complaining is reflexive and takes de: se plaindre de. Il se plaint du temps = complains about the weather (du = de + le).

target: Il s'est endormi devant la télévision.
english: He fell asleep in front of the television.
tip: Dormir is to sleep, but s'endormir is to fall asleep. Il s'est endormi = he dropped off – the reflexive marks the crossing into sleep, not the sleeping itself.

target: Nous cherchons un hôtel qui ait une piscine.
english: We're looking for a hotel that has a pool.
tip: 'Qui ait', not 'qui a': the hotel isn't real yet, you're still searching for one. Wanting something uncertain triggers the subjunctive.

target: Il faut que tout le monde soit prêt à huit heures.
english: Everyone needs to be ready at eight o'clock.
tip: After 'il faut que', être turns into 'soit': 'que tout le monde soit prêt', never 'est'. One of the most irregular subjunctives.

target: Il finira par comprendre.
english: He will end up understanding.
tip: Finir par = to end up doing something. Par introduces the eventual outcome.

target: Elle s'est coupé les ongles.
english: She cut her nails.
tip: Own body parts take 'the', not 'her', in French: s'est coupé les ongles = cut her nails. The reflexive se already tells you whose nails they are, so les does the rest.

target: Je ne le sais pas.
english: I don't know it.
tip: The object pronoun tucks inside the ne...pas wrapper: 'je ne le sais pas'. 'Le' stays glued to the verb, not after 'pas'.

target: Nous nous entendons très bien.
english: We get along very well.
tip: S'entendre literally means 'hear each other', but nous nous entendons très bien = we get along great. In French, getting on well is a matter of hearing each other well.

target: Tu en as assez ?
english: Do you have enough of it?
tip: 'en' stands in for 'of it/some', and French won't drop it the way English does: 'Tu en as assez' is literally 'do you have enough of it'.
